events.description: Art and Art History Under the Tent: Whirling & Flickering August 20-October 15, 2026 Reception: August 20, 5-7 pm Drawn together in graduate school by their mutual love of experimentation and play, Michelle Inez Hinojosa and Barbara Pearsall have built a collaborative practice around analogue animation and vibrant abstraction. Together, their work explores optical toys, immersive installations, and movement. Under the Tent: Whirling & Flickering features kaleidoscopic imagery, flickering abstractions, projection mapping, a hidden trapdoor, and hand-cranked wheels that transform what viewers see. After searching for the perfect venue, they are thrilled to bring their collaborative installation to UNC. Their first public artwork, Turnabout Folly, will debut in Lansing, Michigan in Fall 2026. Michelle Hinojosa works at the intersection of painting, poetry, and fiber art, where she considers memory, intergenerational trauma, and migration. Born in central Texas, by way of the fields of California and Northern Mexico, Michelle uplifts traditions of making that have provided much-needed stability to a family displaced. Michelle Hinojosa is an Assistant Professor of Art at Pennsylvania State University. Barbara Pearsall is an artist and educator based in Michigan. Her art practice is attentive to how deviation from material conventions can subvert or metamorphose the role of institutions, where her philosophical and political concerns manifest through material explorations of the built environment. Her pieces seek to create illusory and unusual architectural conditions as a form of resistance, interrupting real-world functionality to allow for alternative systems of order. She is an Assistant Professor of Foundations & Sculpture at Michigan State University. Admission: Free Gallery Hours: Monday-Friday, 8 am-5 pm A weeknight or daytime permit is now required after 5:00 pm on weekdays. No permit is required from 5:00 pm Friday through 7:30 am Monday. A $1.00 one-night pass is available in selected lots. More information can be found HERE. For more information, please contact: Annette Lawrence, annettel@unc.edu

events.name: Before We Knew Better Art Exhibition
events.description: The Before We Knew Better art exhibition brings together the work of Lamar Whidbee and Chris Facey to reflect on joy, memory and the experiences that shape us early in life. The exhibition looks to childhood as a place of imagination, play and connection. Rather than seeing nostalgia as a way to escape the present, the exhibition considers how memories of joy can remind us of what still matters. Whidbee and Facey ask what we carry with us from those early years and how those experiences continue to influence our well-being, relationships and sense of self. At a time when conversations around mental health are increasingly important, the exhibition offers space to pause, reflect and reconnect with the moments that first taught us about joy. The exhibition will be available for viewing in the art gallery at the African American Cultural Center on weekdays from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. between Aug. 17 and Sept. 25. events.name: Population-Environment: From Challenges to Win-Win Solutions?
events.description: How do human populations impact the environment and how do they respond to environmental change? This talk presents recent research examining how aspects of human population and dynamics impact the environment and, in turn, how they respond to environmental change. Research is presented from rural regions in Latin America, Africa, Asia, and California. Population has long played a key role in environmental change; the environment, in turn, has long impacted human population. However, we still lack an overarching theory of population-environment dynamics. Towards filling this gap, the presentation features case studies, qualitative and quantitative methods, and primary data and secondary data. Analytical methods are largely statistical models with complementary qualitative analyses. Results suggest significant roles that population play directly and indirectly on environmental dynamics and various forms of human population responses to environmental change.

events.description: Special public screening w/ filmmaker Boots Riley in person: "I Love Boosters" (Boots Riley, 2026, 105 min, USA, DCP) == Free parking for this event will be available in the Campus Drive Lot (across from the Rubenstein Arts Center, on Anderson St.) Limited space available, seating will be first come, first served. Doors open 30 min. before show-time. == ABOUT THE FILM: "booster" (n.) - someone who illicitly procures goods from a store and sells them at a discount price Within the aisles of the languishing department stores of Oakland, California, where the townspeople themselves can't afford to step through the front doors, Corvette (Keke Palmer) has a scheme. She and her crew are entering these places, fly but broke, and skittering off with the loot: racks of high-fashion clothing made by the exalted designer Christie Smith (Demi Moore) that they'll redistribute to the masses on the cheap. Call it community service. Corvette wants to be like Christie, an artist who creates these beautiful and daring garments. But the closest she can get to Christie's world is only in disguise, and boosting through the Bay eventually leads Corvette on a consciousness-splitting adventure into new dimensions - and perhaps another way of seeing where she belongs in a bizarre world. From the mad mind of Boots Riley ("Sorry to Bother You"; "I'm a Virgo") comes "I Love Boosters", an electric, mind-bending odyssey through the world of high-fashion and low-rent economies. An outrageously outré vision, Riley's sophomore feature takes us from the malls of Oakland to the factories of China, as Corvette and her fellow boosters, Sade (Naomi Ackie) and Mariah (Taylour Paige), steal their way into a surrealist fantasia that confirms the auteur as an utterly singular voice in contemporary cinema. The film is as stylish as it is humorous and radical. And ultimately, [director Boots Riley] hopes it sparks something beyond the screen: 'I want you to engage with it as a piece of art and come to some conclusions, and hopefully it inspires you to go out and help make a mass, militant, radical labor movement... We need to try to get control of the wealth we have created with our labor.'" -- Jessica Herndon, Sundance Institute == About the filmmaker: Boots Riley is a rapper, songwriter, record producer, filmmaker, and activist whose work operates at the intersection of art & radical politics. [See website for more info.]

events.name: Worlds of 1776 | Sarah Pearsall, “How the World Made the American Revolution”
events.venue: Smith Warehouse, Ahmadieh Family Lecture Hall, Bay 4, C105
events.description: Join us for conversation with Professor Sarah Pearsall (Johns Hopkins University) about her new book Freedom Round the Globe: A World History of the American Revolution In this powerful new history of the American Revolution, Sarah M. S. Pearsall argues that the American Founding Fathers did not have a unique claim on the revolutionary spirit. The thirteen colonies that became the United States, she reminds us, were not even half of the British colonies that existed in the eighteenth century. In her sparkling and original Freedom Round the Globe, Pearsall uncovers the insurgents, freedom lovers, and dreamers in India, West Africa, North America, Europe, China, and West Indian islands who shaped the nature of American rebellion and nationhood. Sarah M.S. Pearsall is Professor and Chair of History at Johns Hopkins University; she previously taught for nearly a decade at Cambridge University. She is the author of four books, including Atlantic Families: Lives and Letters in the Later Eighteenth Century (Oxford University Press, 2008), Polygamy: An Early American History (Yale University Press, 2019), Polygamy: A Very Short Introduction (2022), and most recently, Freedom Round the Globe: A World History of the American Revolution, came out this year with Knopf Doubleday (U.S.), Picador (U.K.), and Rowohlt Berlin (Germany) in 2026. This event is part of the "Worlds of 1776" series, co-sponsored by the Department of History, the John Hope Franklin Humanities Institute, and the Bass Connections "Worlds of 1776" research team. RSVP here.

events.description: Special public screening w/ filmmaker Boots Riley in person: "I Love Boosters" (Boots Riley, 2026, 105 min, USA, DCP) == Free parking for this event will be available in the Campus Drive Lot (across from the Rubenstein Arts Center, on Anderson St.) Limited space available, seating will be first come, first served. Doors open 30 min. before show-time. == ABOUT THE FILM: "booster" (n.) - someone who illicitly procures goods from a store and sells them at a discount price Within the aisles of the languishing department stores of Oakland, California, where the townspeople themselves can't afford to step through the front doors, Corvette (Keke Palmer) has a scheme. She and her crew are entering these places, fly but broke, and skittering off with the loot: racks of high-fashion clothing made by the exalted designer Christie Smith (Demi Moore) that they'll redistribute to the masses on the cheap. Call it community service. Corvette wants to be like Christie, an artist who creates these beautiful and daring garments. But the closest she can get to Christie's world is only in disguise, and boosting through the Bay eventually leads Corvette on a consciousness-splitting adventure into new dimensions - and perhaps another way of seeing where she belongs in a bizarre world. From the mad mind of Boots Riley ("Sorry to Bother You"; "I'm a Virgo") comes "I Love Boosters", an electric, mind-bending odyssey through the world of high-fashion and low-rent economies. An outrageously outré vision, Riley's sophomore feature takes us from the malls of Oakland to the factories of China, as Corvette and her fellow boosters, Sade (Naomi Ackie) and Mariah (Taylour Paige), steal their way into a surrealist fantasia that confirms the auteur as an utterly singular voice in contemporary cinema. The film is as stylish as it is humorous and radical. And ultimately, [director Boots Riley] hopes it sparks something beyond the screen: 'I want you to engage with it as a piece of art and come to some conclusions, and hopefully it inspires you to go out and help make a mass, militant, radical labor movement... We need to try to get control of the wealth we have created with our labor.'" -- Jessica Herndon, Sundance Institute == About the filmmaker: Boots Riley is a rapper, songwriter, record producer, filmmaker, and activist whose work operates at the intersection of art & radical politics. [See website for more info.]

events.address: 121 E. Cameron Avenue, Chapel Hill, NC
events.description: Art and Art History Under the Tent: Whirling & Flickering August 20-October 15, 2026 Reception: August 20, 5-7 pm Drawn together in graduate school by their mutual love of experimentation and play, Michelle Inez Hinojosa and Barbara Pearsall have built a collaborative practice around analogue animation and vibrant abstraction. Together, their work explores optical toys, immersive installations, and movement. Under the Tent: Whirling & Flickering features kaleidoscopic imagery, flickering abstractions, projection mapping, a hidden trapdoor, and hand-cranked wheels that transform what viewers see. After searching for the perfect venue, they are thrilled to bring their collaborative installation to UNC. Their first public artwork, Turnabout Folly, will debut in Lansing, Michigan in Fall 2026. Michelle Hinojosa works at the intersection of painting, poetry, and fiber art, where she considers memory, intergenerational trauma, and migration. Born in central Texas, by way of the fields of California and Northern Mexico, Michelle uplifts traditions of making that have provided much-needed stability to a family displaced. Michelle Hinojosa is an Assistant Professor of Art at Pennsylvania State University. Barbara Pearsall is an artist and educator based in Michigan. Her art practice is attentive to how deviation from material conventions can subvert or metamorphose the role of institutions, where her philosophical and political concerns manifest through material explorations of the built environment. Her pieces seek to create illusory and unusual architectural conditions as a form of resistance, interrupting real-world functionality to allow for alternative systems of order. She is an Assistant Professor of Foundations & Sculpture at Michigan State University. Admission: Free Gallery Hours: Monday-Friday, 8 am-5 pm A weeknight or daytime permit is now required after 5:00 pm on weekdays. No permit is required from 5:00 pm Friday through 7:30 am Monday. A $1.00 one-night pass is available in selected lots. More information can be found HERE. For more information, please contact: Annette Lawrence, annettel@unc.edu

events.name: The Secret Lives and Afterlives of Planktic Foraminifera
events.description: No bigger than a grain of sand, the shells of foraminifera carpet the seafloor and serve as some of Earth’s most remarkable natural archives. For decades, these tiny fossils have helped scientists reconstruct past climates — and may even hold clues to our future. In this talk, we’ll explore the hidden world of foraminifera, how they live, how their shells record the ocean around them and how their fossilized afterlives reveal changes in ocean oxygen through time. Catherine Davis, an associate professor in the Department of Marine, Earth and Atmospheric Sciences, will share some ways we visualize these data, from microscope imagery to global paleoceanographic reconstructions. Davis' talk is part of the NC State University Libraries' Coffee and Viz series. The series gives NC State researchers opportunties to share their visualization work and discuss topics of interest.

events.name: Before We Knew Better Art Exhibition
events.description: The Before We Knew Better art exhibition brings together the work of Lamar Whidbee and Chris Facey to reflect on joy, memory and the experiences that shape us early in life. The exhibition looks to childhood as a place of imagination, play and connection. Rather than seeing nostalgia as a way to escape the present, the exhibition considers how memories of joy can remind us of what still matters. Whidbee and Facey ask what we carry with us from those early years and how those experiences continue to influence our well-being, relationships and sense of self. At a time when conversations around mental health are increasingly important, the exhibition offers space to pause, reflect and reconnect with the moments that first taught us about joy. The exhibition will be available for viewing in the art gallery at the African American Cultural Center on weekdays from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. between Aug. 17 and Sept. 25. Whidbee and Facey will discuss the exhibition during an artist talk event that will be held in the center's art gallery at 6:30 p.m. Sept. 2.

Featuring historical photographs, contemporary images, artworks from the Gregg Museum collection including a handmade guitar by Freeman Vines, and ephemera from community partners, the exhibition reflects on place, memory, creativity, and spiritual resilience across generations. Through stories of triumph and adversity, Community Stories honors the ways Black Americans have sustained and uplifted their communities through family, entrepreneurship, cultural expression, and soulful imagination, while inspiring future generations.

events.name: Agentic Software Development: Staying in Control
events.description: NC State's AI Hub for Science invites you to a hands-on workshop which introduces a disciplined approach to software development with AI coding agents. Participants will learn how to move beyond “vibe coding” by using AI throughout a structured development lifecycle: brainstorming and refining requirements, creating durable specifications, planning work in small testable increments, directing and monitoring coding agents, and verifying their output through testing, review and adversarial analysis. Participants will not only learn to generate code faster, but to specify intent, manage context and constraints, evaluate evidence, and retain human ownership of architecture, risk and the final decision to accept software. The workshop also presents agent skills, showing how reusable instructions and workflows can extend and customize an agent’s capabilities.

events.description: This event is part of "Sharing Ground," a joint NC State–Duke seminar exploring how the humanities can deepen our understanding of academic freedom and the university’s role in sustaining democratic life. events.name: Luminary & Freedom Stories
events.description: During this special luminary program, Bennett Place invites you to reflect on the end of the Civil War as a momentous step towards freedom for all Americans and the end of chattel slavery in the United States. Walk among 3,310 luminaries - one for every 1,000 enslaved people in North Carolina - and reflect on experiences of enslavement and freedom. Historians dot the path and share stories of people's pathways to freedom and life after slavery & the Civil War. --- Harriet Ann Daves recalled just how monumental Civil War surrenders were for her family: "When the surrender came my grandfather came to my mother and told her: 'Well, you are as free as I am.'" Claiming freedom was not so straightforward for the 331,059 enslaved women, children, and men in North Carolina during the Civil War. Some took enormous risk to reach Union lines before the federal government made any promise of abolishing slavery. Others left their homes and plantations to follow Sherman's army as they marched through the southeast. Some believed home was where they already lived and worked and waited patiently for freedom to extend to them. Others still were lied to by their enslavers or moved away from the advancing U.S. Army so they would remain enslaved. Freedom came in different ways and at different times to enslaved people across the state. One common thread unites these freedom stories: the defeat of the Confederate military ensured a new birth of freedom across the state and nation.

events.name: John and June Allcott Gallery: Michelle Inez Hinojosa and Barbara Pearsall
events.address: 121 E. Cameron Avenue, Chapel Hill, NC
events.description: Art and Art History Under the Tent: Whirling & Flickering August 20-October 15, 2026 Reception: August 20, 5-7 pm Drawn together in graduate school by their mutual love of experimentation and play, Michelle Inez Hinojosa and Barbara Pearsall have built a collaborative practice around analogue animation and vibrant abstraction. Together, their work explores optical toys, immersive installations, and movement. Under the Tent: Whirling & Flickering features kaleidoscopic imagery, flickering abstractions, projection mapping, a hidden trapdoor, and hand-cranked wheels that transform what viewers see. After searching for the perfect venue, they are thrilled to bring their collaborative installation to UNC. Their first public artwork, Turnabout Folly, will debut in Lansing, Michigan in Fall 2026. Michelle Hinojosa works at the intersection of painting, poetry, and fiber art, where she considers memory, intergenerational trauma, and migration. Born in central Texas, by way of the fields of California and Northern Mexico, Michelle uplifts traditions of making that have provided much-needed stability to a family displaced. Michelle Hinojosa is an Assistant Professor of Art at Pennsylvania State University. Barbara Pearsall is an artist and educator based in Michigan. Her art practice is attentive to how deviation from material conventions can subvert or metamorphose the role of institutions, where her philosophical and political concerns manifest through material explorations of the built environment. Her pieces seek to create illusory and unusual architectural conditions as a form of resistance, interrupting real-world functionality to allow for alternative systems of order. She is an Assistant Professor of Foundations & Sculpture at Michigan State University. Admission: Free Gallery Hours: Monday-Friday, 8 am-5 pm A weeknight or daytime permit is now required after 5:00 pm on weekdays. No permit is required from 5:00 pm Friday through 7:30 am Monday. A $1.00 one-night pass is available in selected lots. More information can be found HERE. For more information, please contact: Annette Lawrence, annettel@unc.edu

events.name: Before We Knew Better Art Exhibition
events.description: The Before We Knew Better art exhibition brings together the work of Lamar Whidbee and Chris Facey to reflect on joy, memory and the experiences that shape us early in life. The exhibition looks to childhood as a place of imagination, play and connection. Rather than seeing nostalgia as a way to escape the present, the exhibition considers how memories of joy can remind us of what still matters. Whidbee and Facey ask what we carry with us from those early years and how those experiences continue to influence our well-being, relationships and sense of self. At a time when conversations around mental health are increasingly important, the exhibition offers space to pause, reflect and reconnect with the moments that first taught us about joy. The exhibition will be available for viewing in the art gallery at the African American Cultural Center on weekdays from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. between Aug. 17 and Sept. 25. Whidbee and Facey will discuss the exhibition during an artist talk event that will be held in the center's art gallery at 6:30 p.m. Sept. 2.

events.name: Community Stories: Sustaining North Carolina’s Black Heritage
events.description: Community Stories: Sustaining North Carolina’s Black Heritage at the Gregg Museum of Art & Design presents a series of vignettes exploring spaces of dignity, belonging, safety, and imagination within Black communities across North Carolina. Featuring historical photographs, contemporary images, artworks from the Gregg Museum collection including a handmade guitar by Freeman Vines, and ephemera from community partners, the exhibition reflects on place, memory, creativity, and spiritual resilience across generations. Through stories of triumph and adversity, Community Stories honors the ways Black Americans have sustained and uplifted their communities through family, entrepreneurship, cultural expression, and soulful imagination, while inspiring future generations.

events.name: The 1776 North Carolina Constitution
events.description: North Carolina’s 1776 Constitution grew out of two crises: an east-west power struggle that erupted into the War of the Regulation, and a fight for political representation against an increasingly hostile English government. This lecture traces that story back to the religious and political conflicts of 17th-century Britain, through the migrations and economic pressures that shaped colonial North Carolina, to the document that remains the state’s constitutional foundation today. The lecture is presented by an interdisciplinary team from Carolina Law, the History Department and the University Libraries.

events.name: Lectures in Art History: Art, Health, Equity Series featuring Amanda Cachia, Arizona State University
events.address: 205 S. Columbia Street, Chapel Hill, NC
events.description: “Access, Activism, and Aesthetic Revision: Crip Methods for Art History” This talk brings together the core arguments of The Agency of Access: Contemporary Disability Art and Institutional Critique (2024), Hospital Aesthetics: Disability, Medicine, Activism (2025), and Rehabilitating the Asylum: Mental Health Justice and Contemporary Art (2027) to demonstrate that disability is not peripheral to canonical art; instead, it is one of its most generative methodological engines to arise with the canon of 20th century art history. Across these three books, Amanda Cachia develops what she calls a critical-aesthetic approach to access, care, and confinement, tracing how hospitals, asylums, and contemporary art institutions function as overlapping architectures of power, creativity, and resistance. Moving between art history, disability studies, medical humanities, institutional critique, and the activist strategies of contemporary disability artists, Cachia shows how access operates as an artistic medium and how care becomes an aesthetic category. By centering disability as both method and material, she proposes an art history that is structurally transformed by the politics and poetics of access, and how pertinent historical artworks and movements can be reconfigured based on a crip revision. Amanda Cachia is Professor of Practice in Museum Studies in the School of Art at the Herberger Institute for Design and the Arts at Arizona State University and Affiliate Faculty in the Disability Studies B.A. Her research interests include disability art history, theory and activism, crip curatorial practices and access aesthetics, museums, institutional critique, and social justice, and critical disability approaches to translation, movement, medicine, and health. Cachia is the author of three books, Rehabilitating the Asylum: Mental Health Justice and Contemporary Art, (forthcoming 2027), Hospital Aesthetics: Disability, Medicine, Activism (2025), and The Agency of Access: Contemporary Disability Art and Institutional Critique (2024), the latter of which was shortlisted for the College Art Association’s 2026 Charles Rufus Morey Book Award. She is also editor of Curating Access: Disability Art Activism and Creative Accommodation (2022), which includes over 40 international contributors. She is currently working on her fourth book project, Disability Art: A Political History. Since 2010, Cachia has organized 20 art exhibitions devoted to the work of disabled artists. She is currently developing the major touring exhibition Vital Signs: From Patient to Power with Mid-America Arts Alliance and ExhibitsUSA, which will be hosted by numerous galleries across the United States from 2027-2032. Cachia is also a curatorial and disability advisor for a major exhibition being developed about art and disability from the 19th century to the present at the Los Angeles County Museum of Art in 2028.
